abstract: This study examines generative AI's impact on employment using data from Upwork, a major online freelancing platform. Following the releases of image-based models (DALL-E2, Midjourney) in early 2022 and ChatGPT in November 2022, freelancers in AI-exposed occupations experienced a 2% decline in monthly contracts and a 5% drop in earnings. Notably, experienced, high-skill freelancers were disproportionately affected, suggesting AI compresses performance differences across skill levels rather than complementing elite workers as past technologies did.
keyFindings: Freelancers in occupations exposed to generative AI experienced a 2% decline in the number of new monthly contracts following AI model releases in 2022.
Earnings for affected freelancers dropped approximately 5% in total monthly earnings on the platform, with negative effects persisting over 6-8 months.
High-skill and experienced freelancers were disproportionately affected compared to lower-skill workers, reversing historical patterns where advanced technology complemented skilled labor.
The negative effects were comparable in magnitude to automation impacts from industrial robots and policy interventions like minimum wage changes.
Generative AI appears to 'level the playing field' by enabling lower-rated freelancers to produce outputs approximating top-tier quality, reducing premium pricing for experienced workers.
methodology: Empirical study published in Organization Science using data from Upwork, a major online freelancing platform. The analysis employs natural experiments using the launches of image-based AI models (DALL-E2 and Midjourney, early 2022) and text-based model (ChatGPT, November 2022) as exogenous shocks. Researchers compared changes in freelancer outcomes in AI-affected versus less-affected occupations before and after AI launches, examining approximately 6-8 months of post-release data. Occupations were classified by exposure level (e.g., copyeditors and proofreaders as text-exposed; graphic designers as image-exposed; administrative services and video editing as low-exposure). Analysis includes examination of worker characteristics including experience level, client feedback, contract history, and reputational metrics.
qualifiers: The study examines only freelance markets and may not fully capture dynamics of traditional employment arrangements or long-term contractual relationships. Analysis covers only the first 6-8 months following AI model releases, and authors acknowledge that predicting AI's future trajectory remains difficult as the technology continues to evolve rapidly. Findings focus on well-defined, task-oriented freelance jobs arguably more amenable to AI substitution. The authors note that while their data shows persistent negative trends through the observation period, longer-term effects and potential job creation in other sectors remain uncertain.
